summary: Describes IRIS, an XML-based client-server protocol that provides a framework for query and result operations of Internet registry information services. It defines generic operations and a mechanism for extending them to specific registry types.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a common way to ask the Internet's official lists, such as who owns a name, with the same style of question for each list.

questions: what is a search continuation in iris
subtitle: An XML framework for asking Internet registries questions, with room for each kind of registry to define its own.

tldr.problem: Internet registries, such as those for domain names and addresses, each need a way to be queried and return results, and a single common framework avoids reinventing the basics for every registry.
tldr.mechanism: IRIS defines XML request and response documents with generic lookup and search operations, referrals between servers, and extension through XML schemas identified by URNs, plus an iris: URI scheme for naming entities.
tldr.outcome: On its own the core is of limited use; it is a base that registry types (such as domain registries) and transport mappings (such as BEEP) build on.

today: RFC 3981 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2005 and is updated by RFC 4992. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What IRIS Is
sections.content:
The Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS) is an application layer client-server protocol, written in XML, that describes the query types and result types of Internet registry information services. It is a framework: it does not define any particular registry, only the elements needed to identify a registry and to build queries and results.

Each kind of registry is a registry type, identified by a URN that is also the XML namespace of the schema describing its queries, results and entity classes. A server may serve several registry types, and each one it serves is a registry service instance.

The framework has three layers: registry-specific (queries, results and entity classes), common-registry (the base operations and referrals that IRIS defines) and application-transport (authentication, message passing and sessions, for example BEEP).
sections.plainLanguage: IRIS is a shared form for asking questions of official lists. Each kind of list adds its own questions, and how the form gets delivered is a separate matter.

sections.title: Requests and Responses
sections.content:
Every request has a root element <request> and every response has the root <response>. A request holds an optional <control> element and a set of <searchSet> elements. A search set contains either a <lookupEntity> (with attributes registryType, entityClass and entityName) or a query derived from the abstract <query> element.

A response holds an optional <reaction>, a set of <resultSet> elements and an optional <bags> element. Each result set has an <answer>, an optional <additional> section and any errors. Servers MUST return direct answers in <answer> and MAY put referenced, related results in <additional>, which can save the client a second query.

Errors include <nameNotFound>, <invalidName>, <invalidSearch>, <queryNotSupported>, <limitExceeded>, <insufficientResources> and <permissionDenied>, plus three for bags.
sections.plainLanguage: You send a form with your questions in it, and the server sends back a form with answers, extra helpful bits, and a note if something went wrong.

sections.title: Entities, Referrals and Extension
sections.content:
Results are about entities. An entity class groups entities of a kind, and names are unique within a class, so the name 192.0.2.0 can mean a name server in one class and a network in another. IRIS reserves two classes that MUST be valid in every registry type: local for locally defined entities and iris for the service instance, which MUST contain the names id (a <serviceIdentification> result) and limits (a <limits> result describing queries, results and sessions allowed per second, minute, hour or day).

There are two kinds of referral. An entity reference points to a specific entity, and a search continuation lets a search carry on at another server. Clients SHOULD follow an entity or search continuation only once, to avoid a referral loop.

Registry schemas extend IRIS by deriving from the abstract <query> and <result> elements. The identifier of a registry type MUST be the same URN as its XML namespace, and may be abbreviated, so urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:dreg1 can be written dreg1 outside of XML URI contexts.
sections.plainLanguage: Things in a list are filed in drawers (classes). If the answer is in another library, the server hands you a note saying where to go, and you should only follow each note once so you do not walk in circles.

sections.title: Controls and Relay Bags
sections.content:
A <control> lets a client ask for special processing without re-versioning IRIS. The one control defined here, <onlyCheckPermissions>, asks the server only to check whether permissions suffice to run the queries. The server MUST answer with a <standardReaction> containing <controlAccepted>, <controlDenied>, <controlDisabled> or <controlUnrecognized>.

Bags let one server pass opaque data to another through the client. The response carries <bag> elements with an id, referrals point to them with bagRef, and the client MUST NOT assume anything about a bag's contents and MUST include the referenced bag when following the referral. A server MUST NOT ignore a bag it receives, and returns one of <bagUnrecognized>, <bagUnacceptable> or <bagRefused> if it cannot accept it.

Section 5 also defines a <serialization> element for saving a database of IRIS entities and referrals to file storage as XML.
sections.plainLanguage: A bag is a sealed envelope. One server gives it to you, you carry it without peeking, and hand it to the next server.

sections.title: The IRIS URI
sections.content:
An IRIS URI has a rigid shape: iris:<registry>/<resolution>/<authority>/<class>/<name>. It MUST NOT be relative. If the class and name are left out, the defaults iris and id are implied, so iris:dreg1//com means iris:dreg1//com/iris/id. If the resolution method is empty, direct resolution is used.

In direct resolution the authority is a domain name or IP address, optionally with a port. A bare domain name uses the S-NAPTR service location process (NAPTR and SRV records in DNS) to find servers and transports, falling back to A or AAAA records and the well-known port of the transport. An IP address is used directly. Transport-specific schemes such as iris.beep may be defined, and otherwise the default transport specified by IRIS over BEEP (RFC 3983) MUST be used.
sections.plainLanguage: An IRIS address is like a full mailing address for a record: which kind of list, who runs it, which drawer, and what name to look for.

sections.title: Security and Internationalization
sections.content:
The IRIS XML layer provides no authentication or privacy facilities of its own. It relies on the application-transport layer, and transport mappings should explicitly define their security mechanisms. Because referrals can cause a client to query another registry, clients SHOULD NOT use authentication credentials and mechanisms subject to replay attacks for those follow-up lookups.

IRIS is XML, so UTF-8 and UTF-16 are recognized, and UTF-8 is RECOMMENDED. The application-transport layer MUST define a common set of character encodings, and entity definitions SHOULD use the XML language type to help localization.
sections.plainLanguage: The form itself has no lock. The delivery service has to provide the lock, and you should not hand your key to every new office a note sends you to.

layers.label: Registry-Specific
layers.detail: Queries, results and entity classes of one registry type (domain, address, ...)

layers.detail: Base operations, search sets, result sets and referrals

layers.detail: Authentication, message passing and sessions (for example BEEP)
